prompt: A report is slow. Before changing anything, what does the course's first lesson tell you to do?

choices.text: Add an index on every column in its WHERE clause
choices.why: That is a fix for one suspect applied before knowing which.

choices.text: Double the server's memory
choices.why: A bigger machine does nothing for a query that reads too much.

choices.text: Rewrite it as a stored procedure
choices.why: Moving the SQL changes nothing about which suspect it is.

choices.text: Name the suspect first
choices.why: Right: the fixes do not transfer, so the suspect comes first.

prompt: The first run of a query after a restart takes 435 ms, the next two 167 and 208 ms. Which statement about these numbers is right?

choices.text: The first was cold; the gap between the other two is noise
choices.why: Right: the restart and dropped cache made the first read from the disk.

choices.text: The plan changed between the first run and the second
choices.why: Same query, same plan, same rows; only where the bytes were changed.

choices.text: The third run shows the query is getting slower over time
choices.why: 41 ms between two warm runs is the noise the lesson measured.

choices.text: The average, 270 ms, is the number to quote
choices.why: A cold run mixed into warm ones is exactly what not to average.

prompt: Why does `WHERE date(placed_at) = '2025-06-01'` not use the index on `placed_at`?

choices.text: June has too many orders
choices.why: The day held 2801 orders out of two million.

choices.text: The index lists placed_at, not its date
choices.why: Right: ask in the index's own terms, a range of placed_at.

choices.text: Indexes cannot be used for dates
choices.why: The range on placed_at used it in 1.3 ms.

choices.text: The table is too small for an index to be worth it
choices.why: It has two million rows.

prompt: `market` takes 1334 MB and `shared_buffers` is 128 MB. Roughly how many times bigger is the database than PostgreSQL's own cache? Round to the nearest whole number.
Which `pg_stat_statements` sort finds the statements worth fixing first?

choices.text: By total_exec_time, then read the mean
choices.why: Right: candidates by total, then the mean says what each user gains.

choices.text: By calls, most frequent first
choices.why: A frequent statement can be almost free.

choices.text: By queryid
choices.why: queryid is an identifier, not a cost.

choices.text: By mean_exec_time, slowest first
choices.why: The mean says how long one user waits, not what the server spends.

prompt: Why does `pg_stat_statements` store `WHERE customer_id = $1` instead of each customer's number?

choices.text: To hide customers' data from the DBA
choices.why: Hiding is a side effect; the reason is grouping.

choices.text: So a million calls with different values are one row
choices.why: Right: one statement, one row, a large count.

choices.text: Because the server never sees the values
choices.why: It executes them, and the log can record them.

choices.text: To save the time spent parsing
choices.why: It is about the record, not about parsing.

prompt: A tally shows one statement at 0.1 ms called 30 000 times a minute and another at 200 ms called once an hour. You can halve either. Which gives the server more time back?

choices.text: Neither, because both are under a second
choices.why: What matters is the total, not each run.

choices.text: The 200 ms one
choices.why: Halving it saves 100 ms an hour.

choices.text: The 0.1 ms one, by far
choices.why: Right: 0.05 ms × 30 000 a minute is 1.5 s every minute.

choices.text: They are about the same
choices.why: One is seconds a minute, the other milliseconds an hour.

prompt: Put the loop the course repeats in order.
items: Run the workload and read the tally by total
Run the same workload for the same time and compare
trap: Each measurement needs its own clean start, and the change sits between two identical measurements.

prompt: Which question needs the log rather than `pg_stat_statements`?

choices.text: How many times the dashboard ran today
choices.why: calls answers that.

choices.text: The dashboard's mean time
choices.why: mean_exec_time is exactly that.

choices.text: Which statement costs the server the most
choices.why: That is the tally sorted by total.

choices.text: Which seller one slow dashboard run was for
choices.why: Right: the log keeps the values.

prompt: At 900 transactions a second the average latency was 29 ms; at 1050 it was 133 ms, with a maximum of 1099. What is the right reading?

choices.text: The server is near the knee of the curve
choices.why: Right: a sixth more work, four and a half times the latency.

choices.text: The disk is failing at higher rates
choices.why: Nothing points at the disk; this is queueing.

choices.text: 1050 is above the maximum, so the run is invalid
choices.why: 1050 is below 1099.

choices.text: Latency grows in proportion to load
choices.why: It grows slowly and then suddenly, not in proportion.

prompt: A table grows by 2 GB a month and its disk has 50 GB free. How many months until it is full, if nothing else changes?
Why should an alert on an `integer` key's sequence fire about a year before it runs out, while a disk alert can fire weeks ahead?

choices.text: Sequences grow faster than disks
choices.why: How fast they grow is measured separately for each.

choices.text: The disk alert is always ignored anyway
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so.

choices.text: Sequences are more important than disks
choices.why: The difference is the fix, not importance.

choices.text: The fix, moving the key to bigint, rewrites the table and needs planning
choices.why: Right: the alert's lead time is the fix's duration plus a margin.

prompt: Which of these are walls that `capacity.sql` reads from inside the database? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The age of the oldest unfrozen transaction id
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Each sequence against its maximum
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Free space on the disk
choices.why: The database cannot see it; df can.

choices.text: Connections against max_connections
choices.why: Right.

prompt: A new index made a query 0.018 ms faster per call; the write latency before and after overlapped entirely. What may you conclude about its cost on writes?

choices.text: That it has none
choices.why: Not shown is not zero.

choices.text: Nothing: the measurement was too coarse
choices.why: Right: the cost has to be measured another way, in space and per write.

choices.text: That writes became faster
choices.why: Overlapping ranges show no direction.

choices.text: That it doubled the cost of writes
choices.why: A doubling would show far outside the range.

prompt: A change saves 2 ms per call on a statement that runs 50 times a second. How many seconds of server time does it save per hour?
Two runs before a change gave 1134 and 1151 transactions a second; two after gave 1200 and 1116. What is the verdict under the lesson's rule?

choices.text: A loss of 3%
choices.why: That picks the opposite pair.

choices.text: Exactly no change
choices.why: Overlap means not shown, not proven equal.

choices.text: Not shown: the ranges overlap
choices.why: Right: more or longer runs are the way to find out.

choices.text: A 6% improvement
choices.why: That picks the best after against the worst before.

prompt: Before dropping an index, keep the statement that rebuilds it, which the function named `pg_get_` followed by ___ prints.
Which join method fits a handful of outer rows with an index on the inner table's join column?

choices.text: Nested loop
choices.why: Right: one index lookup per outer row is cheap when the rows are few.

choices.text: Hash join
choices.why: Building a hash of the whole inner table costs more than a few lookups.

choices.text: Merge join
choices.why: Sorting both sides is wasted on a handful of rows.

choices.text: Cross join
choices.why: That is every pair, not a join method the planner picks.

prompt: A hash join shows `Batches: 8` with `work_mem` at 1MB and `Batches: 1` at 32MB. What does a batch count above 1 mean?

choices.text: Eight indexes were used
choices.why: A hash join uses no index for the join itself.

choices.text: The hash spilled past work_mem
choices.why: Right: whether that is slower has to be measured, and in the lesson one batch was not the fastest.

choices.text: The join ran on eight parallel workers
choices.why: Workers are shown separately; batches are about memory.

choices.text: The join was repeated eight times
choices.why: That would be loops.

prompt: The planner chose a hash join at 1392 ms over a merge join that ran in 171 ms, with row estimates within 1%. What was the wrong input?

choices.text: work_mem was too large
choices.why: Memory decides batches, not which method wins here.

choices.text: The statistics were stale
choices.why: Fresh statistics gave estimates within 1%.

choices.text: random_page_cost
choices.why: Right: with 1.1 the planner picked the merge; the estimates were never the problem.

choices.text: The row estimates
choices.why: They were within 1%.

prompt: As the number of customers in a join grows, put the methods the lesson saw the planner choose in order.
trap: Per-row lookups win while the outer side is small; a hash wins once building it is cheaper than that many lookups.

prompt: In `cost=0.43..68618.43`, what is the first number?

choices.text: The cost before the node hands up its first row
choices.why: Right: the startup cost; the second is the total.

choices.text: The milliseconds the node will take to start
choices.why: Costs are in the planner's own units, not milliseconds.

choices.text: The fraction of the table it reads
choices.why: That is not what a cost is.

choices.text: The cost of the cheapest alternative plan
choices.why: A plan shows only the chosen plan's costs.

prompt: An inner node shows `actual time=0.012..0.012 rows=1 loops=25000`. What did it cost in all?
hint: Lesson 3. The times are per loop.

choices.text: Nothing: loops count retries that were discarded
choices.why: Every loop did real work.

choices.text: About 0.012 ms
choices.why: That is one loop; there were 25000.

choices.text: About 300 ms and 25000 rows
choices.why: Right: times and rows are averages per loop, so multiply.

choices.text: About 25 seconds

prompt: Why wrap `EXPLAIN ANALYZE UPDATE …` in `BEGIN` and `ROLLBACK`?

choices.text: To make the timings more accurate
choices.why: The transaction does not change the measurement.

choices.text: Because UPDATE plans are only shown inside a transaction
choices.why: Plain EXPLAIN UPDATE shows the plan without running it.

choices.text: ANALYZE really runs the statement
choices.why: Right: the rows are changed, and the rollback undoes it.

choices.text: EXPLAIN refuses to run outside a transaction
choices.why: It runs anywhere.

prompt: A table has `relpages` 1000 and `reltuples` 100000. With `seq_page_cost` 1 and `cpu_tuple_cost` 0.01, what total cost does a plain sequential scan with no condition print?
hint: Lesson 3. Pages times one, plus rows times 0.01.

prompt: You want to know whether a rewritten report does less work, on a shared server whose cache changes all day. What do you compare?

choices.text: Execution Time of one run each
choices.why: Timings move with the cache and the neighbours.

choices.text: The pages touched, hit plus read, at the top node
choices.why: Right: the count of pages does not depend on where they were found.

choices.text: The cost on the top line
choices.why: Two different queries' costs are not comparable that way.

choices.text: The number of nodes in the plan
choices.why: A longer plan can do less work.

prompt: Seller 42 is not on `most_common_vals` for `orders.seller_id`. How is its count estimated?

choices.text: As one row, the default for unknown values
choices.why: The estimate was 1491.

choices.text: The leftover share, split evenly
choices.why: Right: 0.7382 of the table over 990 values, 1491 rows.

choices.text: From the histogram of seller_id
choices.why: The lesson's arithmetic uses the list and n_distinct.

choices.text: It is read from the index
choices.why: Estimates come from pg_statistic, not by reading the index.

prompt: Curitiba is 0.0685 of customers and PR is 0.0685. Without extended statistics, what does the planner expect for `city = 'Curitiba' AND state = 'PR'`?

choices.text: Too many: it adds the fractions
choices.why: AND multiplies; it does not add.

choices.text: Zero, because the two conditions conflict
choices.why: They do not conflict; they agree.

choices.text: Far too few: it multiplies the fractions
choices.why: Right: 938 expected, while every Curitiba customer is in PR.

choices.text: Exactly the right number
choices.why: Independence is wrong for two columns that say one thing.

prompt: With `default_statistics_target` at 100, how many rows does ANALYZE sample from a table?
Match each `pg_stats` field to what it describes.

pairs.right: the values frequent enough to be listed
bucket edges holding equal numbers of rows
how many different values, or a negative fraction
how closely physical order follows the column's order

right_distractors: how often the column is updated

prompt: A table of readings has `sensor_id` and `site_id`, and each sensor belongs to one site. `WHERE site_id = 7 AND sensor_id = 70` is estimated at 3 rows and returns 4000. What fixes the estimate?

choices.text: VACUUM FULL
choices.why: Rewriting the table changes nothing about the assumption.

choices.text: A bigger default_statistics_target on both columns
choices.why: Better single-column numbers are still multiplied as if independent.

choices.text: An index on both columns
choices.why: An index speeds the read but does not change the estimate.

choices.text: Extended statistics on the pair, then ANALYZE
choices.why: Right: dependencies tell the planner sensor fixes site.

prompt: A month of orders (4.5% of the table) gets an index scan and a hundred customers (0.05%) get a bitmap scan. What explains it?

choices.text: customer_id has no index
choices.why: The bitmap scan used orders_customer_id_idx.

choices.text: The month was cached and the customers were not
choices.why: Plans are chosen from statistics, not from what is cached.

choices.text: Correlation: the month's rows share pages
choices.why: Right: placed_at follows the physical order; customer_id does not.

choices.text: The planner always prefers bitmaps for small results
choices.why: A month is the larger result and got the index scan.

prompt: A bitmap heap scan shows `Heap Blocks: exact=635 lossy=16032` and a large `Rows Removed by Index Recheck`. What happened?

choices.text: The index is corrupt
choices.why: Lossy pages are a memory limit, not damage.

choices.text: The table needs ANALYZE
choices.why: Statistics do not decide how big the bitmap may grow.

choices.text: Another session held a lock on those pages
choices.why: Reads do not wait on page locks like that.

choices.text: The bitmap outgrew `work_mem`
choices.why: Right: every row on a lossy page has to be checked again.

prompt: A colleague puts `SET enable_seqscan = off` in the application's connection setup because one report got faster. What is the course's verdict?

choices.text: Fine, as long as the report is the most important query
choices.why: It changes every query on those connections.

choices.text: Wrong: every query loses its right sequential scans, and the real misestimate stays
choices.why: Right: the setting is for comparing plans, never a fix.

choices.text: Wrong only because it needs a restart
choices.why: It is a session setting; that is not the problem.

choices.text: Fine, because the planner ignores it when a scan is cheaper
choices.why: It adds a large penalty to every sequential scan.

prompt: `CREATE INDEX ON orders (placed_at) WHERE status = 'pending'`. Which query can use it?

choices.text: `count(*)` of all orders
choices.why: The index holds only the pending ones.

choices.text: `count(*) WHERE status = 'pending'`
choices.why: Right: the query's condition implies the index's.

choices.text: `count(*) WHERE status <> 'pending'`
choices.why: Those are exactly the rows the index leaves out.

choices.text: `count(*) WHERE status = $1`, generic plan, run with 'pending'
choices.why: A generic plan must cover every status.

prompt: Why does PostgreSQL refuse `CREATE INDEX ON orders (date(placed_at))`?

choices.text: placed_at already has an index
choices.why: A column may have several indexes.

choices.text: Dates cannot be indexed
choices.why: The AT TIME ZONE expression was indexed.

choices.text: It depends on the TimeZone setting
choices.why: Right: it is not IMMUTABLE, so an index could hold answers that change.

choices.text: Functions cannot appear in an index
choices.why: lower(email) was indexed in the same lesson.

prompt: The full index on `status` was 13 MB and the partial one for pending orders 176 kB. About how many times smaller is the partial one? (1 MB = 1024 kB, round to the nearest ten)
A plan says `Index Only Scan` with `Heap Fetches: 87062` out of about a hundred thousand rows. How should you read it?

choices.text: As mostly an ordinary index scan
choices.why: Right: most rows still went to the table, because their pages were not all-visible.

choices.text: As a fast plan, because the node's name says so
choices.why: The name is the plan's intention; Heap Fetches is what happened.

choices.text: As a corrupted visibility map
choices.why: Recent changes clear bits; nothing is corrupt.

choices.text: As a sign the index is missing a column
choices.why: A missing column would rule out an index-only scan altogether.

prompt: What sets a page's bit in the visibility map, and what clears it?

choices.text: CREATE INDEX sets it; DROP INDEX clears it
choices.why: The map belongs to the table, not to an index.

choices.text: VACUUM sets it; a row change clears it
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: ANALYZE sets it; a read clears it
choices.why: ANALYZE samples; reads change nothing.

choices.text: A checkpoint sets it; a restart clears it
choices.why: Neither is what moves those bits.

prompt: Columns a query only returns, and never searches or sorts on, go after the key in an ___ clause.
An `ALTER TABLE` waits behind a long `SELECT`, and every new `SELECT` on the table waits behind the `ALTER`. What is the defence the lesson names?

choices.text: Raising max_connections
choices.why: More connections join the same queue.

choices.text: Running the ALTER with NOWAIT on every SELECT
choices.why: NOWAIT is for row locks in SELECT FOR UPDATE.

choices.text: Running VACUUM first
choices.why: VACUUM does not release anybody's lock.

choices.text: `lock_timeout` of a few seconds, and retry
choices.why: Right: a short wait that gives up keeps the queue from forming.

prompt: A finance report uses `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` "so that it never waits". What is wrong?

choices.text: Locked rows are silently skipped
choices.why: Right: SKIP LOCKED is for a job queue, where any free row will do.

choices.text: SKIP LOCKED only works on primary keys
choices.why: It works on any rows the query locks.

choices.text: Reports cannot take row locks
choices.why: Any query can.

choices.text: It makes the report wait longer
choices.why: It makes it wait less, at the price of missing rows.

prompt: Put the steps of a deadlock between two windows in order.
items: Window A asks for order 2 and waits
Window B asks for order 1 and waits
After deadlock_timeout, one of them is cancelled
trap: Each must hold one row before asking for the other's; detection only runs after the timeout.

prompt: A customer cancels an order, the page reloads from a replica 10 seconds behind, and the order shows as still open. What property was broken?

choices.text: Isolation between two transactions
choices.why: The problem is a copy behind, not two transactions colliding.

choices.text: The replica's indexes
choices.why: The replica has the same indexes; it was behind.

choices.text: Reading your own writes
choices.why: Right: the fix waits for the replica to replay past the write's LSN, or reads the primary.

choices.text: Durability
choices.why: The cancel was committed on the primary.

prompt: A team turns on `hot_standby_feedback` so a six-hour export on the replica stops failing. A week later the primary's busiest tables have grown. Why?

choices.text: The replica sends its own writes back to the primary
choices.why: A standby writes nothing.

choices.text: Feedback doubles the WAL the primary writes
choices.why: It sends a horizon, not data.

choices.text: The export copies the tables into the primary
choices.why: Nothing is copied back.

choices.text: It holds back VACUUM on the primary
choices.why: Right: the replica's snapshot now holds the primary's horizon.

prompt: Without feedback, a long query on the replica was cancelled with `canceling statement due to conflict with ___`.
In a plan read from the bottom, where does the misestimate that matters start?

choices.text: At any join
choices.why: A join usually inherits its inputs' errors.

choices.text: At the lowest node where estimated and actual rows part
choices.why: Right: the nodes above it only inherit the error.

choices.text: At the top node, which has the biggest numbers
choices.why: The top only shows the sum of what went wrong below.

choices.text: At the slowest node
choices.why: Slowness can be a consequence of an estimate made lower down.

prompt: After 300,000 orders were imported with autovacuum off, at about how many changed rows would autoanalyze have run on `orders` (2,000,000 rows, threshold 50, scale factor 0.1)?
hint: Lesson 6. Threshold plus factor times rows.

prompt: After a bulk import of pending orders, `status = 'pending'` was estimated at 7590 and returned 307,319, and the plan became a long nested loop. What fixed it, and what prevents it next time?

choices.text: An index on status, so the scan is cheap
choices.why: An index does not change the estimate the plan was built on.

choices.text: VACUUM FULL, so the table is compact again
choices.why: Rewriting the table does not refresh the statistics.

choices.text: More work_mem, so the plan fits in memory
choices.why: Memory changes a spill, not the estimate.

choices.text: ANALYZE, now and after each bulk load
choices.why: Right: the old fraction of pending rows was the stale part.

prompt: Which index type answers `tags @> ARRAY['kitchen']` on `products`?

choices.text: GIN
choices.why: Right: for each tag, the rows that contain it.

choices.text: A B-tree on tags
choices.why: A B-tree orders whole arrays; it cannot look inside one.

choices.text: Hash
choices.why: Hash answers only = on the whole value.

choices.text: BRIN
choices.why: BRIN keeps a minimum and a maximum per range of pages.

prompt: A BRIN index on `events.at` worked and one on `events.customer_id` took 445 ms for one customer. Which statistic told the difference in advance?

choices.text: most_common_freqs
choices.why: Frequencies say how often, not where.

choices.text: n_distinct
choices.why: How many values there are does not say how they are laid out.

choices.text: correlation
choices.why: Right: near 1 for at, about zero for customer_id.

choices.text: null_frac
choices.why: Nulls are not what made it slow.

prompt: A `LIKE 'user42@%'` on a column with a unique B-tree gets a sequential scan. What is the cause?

choices.text: Unique indexes are only for constraints, never for reads
choices.why: The planner reads unique indexes like any other.

choices.text: The table needs VACUUM before the index is trusted
choices.why: Vacuum does not decide whether an index can answer LIKE.

choices.text: The collation; it needs `text_pattern_ops`
choices.why: Right: under another collation the index's order is not a character order.

choices.text: LIKE can never use an index, whatever the pattern
choices.why: With text_pattern_ops the same LIKE used one.

prompt: Why does an index that no query reads still cost something on a table that takes writes?

choices.text: The planner wastes time considering it on every read
choices.why: Planning cost exists, but the lesson measured the writes.

choices.text: It is rebuilt every night
choices.why: Nothing rebuilds indexes on a schedule by itself.

choices.text: It locks the table while unused
choices.why: An unused index takes no locks.

choices.text: Every write updates it too
choices.why: Right: in the lesson the log per order nearly doubled with the leftovers.

prompt: An index shows `idx_scan = 0` on the primary. Which of these could still mean it is needed? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The counters were reset two days ago and a report runs monthly
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Reports run on a read replica
choices.why: Right: each server counts its own scans.

choices.text: It backs a unique constraint
choices.why: Right: it is used on every insert, without a scan.

choices.text: Its table is large
choices.why: Size says nothing about whether it is read.

prompt: A busy `payments` table has an unread index on `status`, and every payment's status changes. What does dropping it give back besides space?

choices.text: A smaller primary key
choices.why: The primary key is a separate index.

choices.text: HOT updates, which skip writing every index
choices.why: Right: an indexed column changing rules HOT out.

choices.text: Faster reads of payments by id
choices.why: The id lookup uses the primary key either way.

choices.text: Nothing: an unread index costs only space
choices.why: It costs every update that changes status.

prompt: A session opened `REPEATABLE READ`, read a table and went idle for an hour while another updated it constantly. What did VACUUM do meanwhile?

choices.text: Removed them, because the idle session had not written
choices.why: A reader's snapshot holds the horizon too.

choices.text: Waited for a lock on the table
choices.why: VACUUM does not wait on readers' locks.

choices.text: Left the dead versions in place
choices.why: Right: the horizon held, and the table grew.

choices.text: Cancelled the idle session
choices.why: VACUUM never cancels sessions.

prompt: What happens when `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` fires?

choices.text: The transaction is committed
choices.why: Nothing is committed on its behalf.

choices.text: A warning is written and the session goes on
choices.why: It ends the session.

choices.text: Only the current statement is cancelled
choices.why: That is statement_timeout, and an idle session is running none.

choices.text: The session ends with FATAL
choices.why: Right: the whole session, not only the transaction.

prompt: Deleting October from the plain `events` table wrote about 251 MB of WAL; detaching and dropping October's partition wrote 55 kB. Roughly how many times more did the DELETE write? Round to the nearest thousand.
Why must the primary key of a table partitioned by `at` include `at`?

choices.text: Because partitions cannot have indexes otherwise
choices.why: Partitions can have any index; uniqueness is the issue.

choices.text: Each partition checks only its own rows
choices.why: Right: without the key column, two months could hold the same id.

choices.text: Because timestamps are faster to index
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; correctness is.

choices.text: It is a convention, not a rule
choices.why: The CREATE TABLE in the lesson failed without it.

prompt: A nightly `DELETE` of rows older than 90 days on a 400 GB log table takes an hour and makes replicas fall behind. What does the course suggest?

choices.text: Add an index on the date column
choices.why: The DELETE still writes every row it removes.

choices.text: VACUUM FULL after each DELETE
choices.why: That adds a full rewrite and a lock.

choices.text: Run the DELETE in smaller batches during the day
choices.why: That spreads the same work and the same log over the day.

choices.text: Partition by day and drop old days
choices.why: Right: dropping a partition writes almost nothing.

prompt: Which kind of load is the reason sharding exists, because replicas cannot absorb it?

choices.text: Reads
choices.why: Replicas and caches spread reads.

choices.text: Reports
choices.why: Reports are reads, served by a replica.

choices.text: Backups
choices.why: Backups are not why anybody shards.

choices.text: Writes
choices.why: Right: every copy has to apply every write.

prompt: Split by `seller_id % 4`, what percentage of all orders landed on the shard holding seller 1? Use one decimal place.
Two shards are backed up one after the other each night, an hour apart. What does a restore of both lose that one database's restore would not?

choices.text: The sequences of both shards
choices.why: Sequences are restored with each shard.

choices.text: Nothing, if both backups succeeded
choices.why: They come back at two different moments.

choices.text: A single moment: cross-shard transactions come back cut in half
choices.why: Right: one shard holds what the other has not seen.

choices.text: The indexes, which are not backed up
choices.why: Indexes come back with the data.

prompt: During a lock incident a dashboard of `active` queries over five seconds shows nothing. Why?

choices.text: The waits are shorter than five seconds
choices.why: The waiters would show if the filter included them; the root would not.

choices.text: Locks are only visible in the log
choices.why: pg_locks shows them live.

choices.text: The root is idle in transaction, which the filter hides
choices.why: Right: the session holding everybody up is running nothing.

choices.text: pg_stat_activity is empty during lock waits
choices.why: The waiters are listed, with wait_event_type Lock.

prompt: Why does cancelling the waiting session a user complains about not end a blocking chain?

choices.text: Cancelling never works on a waiting session
choices.why: It cancels the wait; it does not remove the cause.

choices.text: The cancelled session restarts its statement automatically
choices.why: Nothing restarts it; the application may.

choices.text: Cancelling escalates the lock to the whole table
choices.why: Locks are not escalated in PostgreSQL.

choices.text: The root still holds its lock
choices.why: Right: act on the root, which blocks somebody and waits for nobody.

prompt: What does `pg_cancel_backend` do to a session that is idle in a transaction?

choices.text: Nothing visible: it has no statement running to cancel
choices.why: Right: pg_terminate_backend ends the session and rolls the transaction back.

choices.text: It commits the transaction
choices.why: Nothing is ever committed on a session's behalf.

choices.text: It ends the session
choices.why: That is pg_terminate_backend.

choices.text: It releases its locks but keeps the transaction
choices.why: Locks last until the transaction ends.

prompt: In `pg_locks`, the column that tells a held lock from one somebody is waiting for is `___`.
Two sessions under READ COMMITTED each read a price of 9290, add 100 in the application and write it back. The price ends at 9390. What fixes it without changing the isolation level?

choices.text: Committing each transaction faster, before the other reads
choices.why: The window shrinks; the lost update stays possible.

choices.text: Running VACUUM between the two
choices.why: VACUUM has nothing to do with lost updates.

choices.text: Add 100 in SQL, or read with FOR UPDATE
choices.why: Right: the arithmetic happens on the current row, or the second reader waits.

choices.text: An index on the price column, so the write is quicker
choices.why: Indexes do not order concurrent writes.

prompt: Under REPEATABLE READ, a session's UPDATE fails with `could not serialize access due to concurrent update`. What must the application do?

choices.text: Retry only the failed UPDATE
choices.why: The snapshot is still old; the whole transaction must start again.

choices.text: Ignore it; the row was updated anyway
choices.why: It was not; the transaction is aborted.

choices.text: Switch the whole server to SERIALIZABLE
choices.why: That raises more of these errors, not fewer.

choices.text: Roll back and run the whole transaction again
choices.why: Right: the retry belongs around the unit of work, not one statement.

prompt: Two sessions each check that a customer has no pending order and then insert one. REPEATABLE READ let both in; SERIALIZABLE stopped the second with 40001. What is this anomaly called?

choices.text: Write skew
choices.why: Right: each read was true when made, and the writes together break the rule.

choices.text: A dirty read
choices.why: PostgreSQL never shows uncommitted data.

choices.text: A deadlock
choices.why: Nobody waited for anybody.

choices.text: A lost update
choices.why: No row was written twice; two new rows were inserted.

prompt: Under READ COMMITTED, the read-modify-write pgbench run committed 55,802 bumps but added only 37,821. How many were lost?
Throughput rose from 489 to about 1400 transactions a second up to 16 clients and then stayed flat to 90, while latency climbed to 61 ms. What does raising `max_connections` to 500 buy?

choices.text: Lower latency for every client
choices.why: Latency rose with clients.

choices.text: Nothing at all, because the setting is ignored
choices.why: It takes effect after a restart; it just does not help.

choices.text: More waiting, not more throughput
choices.why: Right: past the flat part, each new client only queues.

choices.text: About five times the throughput
choices.why: The curve was already flat at 16 clients.

prompt: Through PgBouncer in transaction mode, 200 clients ran while the server saw 9 connections. What does a client lose in that mode?

choices.text: Transactions: each statement commits on its own
choices.why: A transaction stays on one server connection to the end.

choices.text: Authentication
choices.why: Clients still authenticate.

choices.text: Nothing; transaction mode is identical to a direct connection
choices.why: Anything that outlives a transaction can break.

choices.text: Session state, such as a SET
choices.why: Right: the lesson showed it happen.

prompt: Pool sizes of 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32 server connections were measured on the four-processor lab machine, and above 8 the differences were within the noise. What should set a pool's size?

choices.text: A measurement on the server it serves
choices.why: Right: a rule of thumb starts the search; the curve ends it.

choices.text: The number of application clients
choices.why: That is what the pool exists to decouple from.

choices.text: max_connections minus three
choices.why: That is a ceiling, not a good size.

choices.text: Always 100
choices.why: The lab measured nothing gained above 8.

prompt: On a table partitioned by `at`, which condition lets the planner prune partitions?

choices.text: `customer_id = 42`
choices.why: Not the partition key.

choices.text: A range on at itself
choices.why: Right: the key, compared directly, names the partitions.
A function on the key reads every partition.

choices.text: `extract(month FROM at) = 11`
choices.why: Also a function on the key.

prompt: A prepared statement with a generic plan shows `Subplans Removed: 3`. When were those partitions removed?

choices.text: When the partitions were created
choices.why: Pruning is per query.

choices.text: By VACUUM, overnight
choices.why: VACUUM has nothing to do with pruning.

choices.text: At execution, once the parameter's value was known
choices.why: Right: run-time pruning.

choices.text: At planning, from the literal in the SQL
choices.why: A generic plan has no literal, only $1.

prompt: With 365 daily partitions, planning grew from about 1 ms to about 30 ms, and even a pruned query planned slower. What is the lesson for choosing a partition size?

choices.text: More partitions are always faster
choices.why: The measurement says the opposite for planning.

choices.text: Daily partitions are required for pruning
choices.why: Monthly partitions pruned in the lesson.

choices.text: Planning time does not matter on a server
choices.why: 30 ms per query is more than most of the workload's queries take to run.

choices.text: No finer than the removal you need
choices.why: Right: monthly if you drop months.

prompt: In cache-aside, who fills the cache?

choices.text: The application, after a miss
choices.why: Right: it reads the database and stores the answer with a TTL.

choices.text: The database, on every write
choices.why: The database knows nothing about the cache.

choices.text: The cache, by polling the database
choices.why: Redis does not read PostgreSQL on its own.

choices.text: A nightly job
choices.why: Cache-aside fills on demand.

prompt: A seller's dashboard is cached for 60 seconds. A new order arrives at second 10. What do readers see until second 60?

choices.text: Nothing, because the key is deleted on write
choices.why: Only if the application invalidates it; a TTL alone does not.

choices.text: The old count: the TTL is the staleness the cache allows
choices.why: Right: in the lesson the cache said 91 while the database said 92.

choices.text: The new count, because Redis watches the table
choices.why: Nothing tells Redis about the order.

choices.text: An error until the key expires
choices.why: The stale value is served without complaint.

prompt: The application deletes a key on every write, yet a stale value sometimes comes back and stays. How?

choices.text: The TTL resets the deleted key
choices.why: A TTL only removes keys.

choices.text: PostgreSQL replays the old value into Redis
choices.why: The database never writes to the cache.

choices.text: A slow reader re-caches the old value
choices.why: Right: the lesson forced that interleaving and guarded it with a per-key version.

choices.text: Redis ignores DEL under load
choices.why: DEL always runs.

prompt: When a hot key expired, 50 concurrent requests made 50 database queries; with single flight they made how many?
Why did `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY` fail until an index was added?

choices.text: It needs a unique index to match old rows with new ones
choices.why: Right: a concurrent refresh computes a diff, row by row.

choices.text: Materialized views cannot be refreshed without any index
choices.why: A plain REFRESH worked without one.

choices.text: CONCURRENTLY needs superuser
choices.why: The error was about the index, not privileges.

choices.text: The view was too large
choices.why: Size is not the condition.

prompt: With `default_statistics_target` at 100, how many rows does ANALYZE put in its sample of a five-million-row table?

choices.text: From autoanalyze, which ran during the import
choices.why: It was switched off, and last_autoanalyze stayed empty.

choices.text: From n_live_tup in pg_stat_user_tables
choices.why: The planner reads pg_class and the file size, not the activity counters.

choices.text: From the table's current size in pages
choices.why: Right: it scales reltuples by the real page count, so the count is right and the mix is stale.

choices.text: From a quick count it runs when reltuples looks old
choices.why: The planner never counts rows to plan.

prompt: A Sort planned for 7590 rows received 307,319. What happened to it?

choices.text: It spilled to disk as an external merge
choices.why: Right: 7216 kB written, memory planned for an estimate spent on the actual.

choices.text: The planner stopped and replanned it with the right count
choices.why: A plan is fixed once execution starts.

choices.text: It sorted only the first 7590 rows
choices.why: Every row is sorted; the estimate only sized the memory.

choices.text: It failed with an out-of-memory error
choices.why: A sort that outgrows its memory spills; it does not fail.

prompt: In `pg_locks`, which column separates a lock that is held from one that is being waited for?

choices.text: `mode`
choices.why: mode says which kind of lock, held or not.

choices.text: `locktype`
choices.why: locktype says what is locked: a relation, a tuple, a transaction id.

choices.text: `granted`
choices.why: Right: t for held, f for waiting, and the f rows are the problem.

choices.text: `pid`
choices.why: pid says whose lock it is, not whether it was given.

prompt: In a blocking graph built from `pg_blocking_pids`, which session is the root?

choices.text: The session running the longest statement
choices.why: The lesson's root was running no statement at all: idle in transaction.

choices.text: The one that has waited longest
choices.why: The longest waiter is a victim; the root waits for nobody.

choices.text: One that blocks others and waits for nobody
choices.why: Right: an empty blocked_by, and its pid inside somebody else's.

choices.text: The one with the highest pid, since it arrived last
choices.why: pids say nothing about who blocks whom.

prompt: A session inside a long transaction is stuck in a lock wait, and you cancel its statement with `pg_cancel_backend`. Which locks does it still hold?

choices.text: Every lock its transaction took, until it rolls back
choices.why: Right: which is why terminating may be needed after all.

choices.text: Only row locks; table locks are released at once
choices.why: Locks of every kind are released at the end of the transaction, not before.

choices.text: None: cancelling ends the transaction
choices.why: Cancelling fails the statement; the transaction stays open until the client rolls back.

choices.text: Only the lock it was waiting for
choices.why: It never had that one; it was waiting for it.

prompt: With `log_lock_waits = on` and the default `deadlock_timeout`, after how many milliseconds does a waiting session write its first `still waiting` line?

choices.text: A thread inside one shared server process
choices.why: PostgreSQL forks a process per connection, not a thread.

choices.text: A whole operating-system process
choices.why: Right: one per session, visible in ps.

choices.text: Nothing until the first query arrives
choices.why: The process exists, idle, from the moment the client connects.

choices.text: A slot in PgBouncer
choices.why: PgBouncer is a separate program the lesson adds; PostgreSQL knows nothing of it.

prompt: Ninety clients completed 1481 transactions a second. By Little's law, what was the average latency, in milliseconds?

choices.text: 100, the server's max_connections
choices.why: The pool never opens more than its size.

choices.text: Four, one per processor
choices.why: Processors are where the curve bends; the pool size set the count.

choices.text: 200, one per client
choices.why: That is a direct connection; the pool shares eight.

choices.text: Eight; the rest waited in the pooler
choices.why: Right: 192 clients waited in the pooler instead of the server.

prompt: Three application servers each run PgBouncer with `default_pool_size = 30` against one database with `max_connections = 100` on four processors. What does the lesson say is wrong?

choices.why: It can; the problem is the sum of the pools.

choices.text: Ninety busy connections only add waiting, with little room left
choices.why: Right: past the bend, more connections add waiting, not throughput.

choices.why: That would ask for 300 connections from a server that allows 100.

prompt: On a table partitioned by month on `at`, why does `WHERE date(at) = '2025-11-10'` read every partition?

choices.text: Pruning only works with prepared statements
choices.why: A literal range on at pruned to one partition in psql.

choices.text: It is not a range of `at`, so the bounds cannot rule anything out
choices.why: Right: the bounds are values of at, and a function of at is not at.

choices.text: November's partition had no index
choices.why: Pruning uses the partition bounds, not indexes.

choices.text: Statistics on the partitions were stale
choices.why: Pruning compares bounds; statistics do not enter into it.

prompt: An `Append` in a plan shows `Subplans Removed: 3`. What happened?

choices.why: Workers appear as Workers Launched; subplans are partitions.

choices.text: Three partitions were empty
choices.why: Empty partitions are scanned like any other unless pruned.

choices.text: Three partitions were dropped when execution started

choices.text: The planner removed three indexes it judged useless

choices.why: The user gets the real answer on a miss, from the database.

prompt: Of 5000 dashboard requests through the lesson's cache, how many reached the database?

choices.why: That is the worst case; a change can land just before an entry expires.

choices.text: Until the next restart of the cache
choices.why: The TTL ends each entry long before any restart.

choices.text: Not at all, because Redis watches the table
choices.why: Redis never sees the database's writes.

prompt: Fifty requests for one missing key ran the count fifty times, each taking about 1.3 s instead of 55 ms. What fixes the stampede, as the lesson built it?

choices.why: Right: single flight, one count instead of fifty.

choices.text: More processors for the database
choices.why: Fifty identical counts would still run; they would only queue less.

choices.why: That makes misses more frequent, and each one can stampede.
